result.title: Zwei Fahrkarten
result.story:
Mia und Paul stehen am Bahnhof. Mia hat eine Tasche. Paul hat einen Rucksack. Sie wollen zusammen nach Berlin fahren.

„Hast du deine Fahrkarte?“, fragt Mia.

„Ja, hier“, sagt Paul. Er nimmt die Fahrkarte aus seinem Rucksack.

Mia sieht auf ihre Fahrkarte.

„Mein Zug fährt nach Berlin“, sagt sie. „Wohin fährt dein Zug?“

Paul liest seine Fahrkarte.

„Mein Zug fährt nach Bremen.“

Er sieht Mia an.

„Nach Bremen? Ich will auch nach Berlin!“

„Zeig mir deine Fahrkarte“, sagt Mia.

Paul zeigt Mia die Fahrkarte. Mia hält ihre Fahrkarte daneben.

„Hier steht Berlin“, sagt Mia. „Und auf deiner Fahrkarte steht Bremen.“

Paul liest die Namen noch einmal.

„Die Stadt ist anders“, sagt er. „Meine Fahrkarte ist nicht für Berlin.“

„Ja“, sagt Mia. „Wir haben Fahrkarten für zwei verschiedene Städte.“

Paul sieht einen Schalter. Dort sitzt eine Frau.

„Wir brauchen Hilfe“, sagt er.

Mia nickt. Die beiden gehen mit ihren Fahrkarten zum Schalter.

glossary.meaning: And; joins people or statements.
To stand; stehen is the present-tense form used with Mia and Paul together.
At the; short for an dem. Here it gives the location at the station.
Railway station; Bahnhof follows am here.
To have; hat goes with one person, Hast with du in a question, and haben with wir.
A or an; eine is used with feminine nouns, and einen with masculine nouns as direct objects.
Bag.
Backpack.
They or she; Sie refers to both friends at the beginning, while sie later refers to Mia.
To want to; wollen is plural, while will goes with ich. The action verb fahren comes later in the clause.
Together.
To, before a city name; marks the destination of a journey.
To travel or go by transport; fährt means a train goes to a destination.
You, when speaking informally to one person.
Your, when addressing one person informally; dein goes with Zug, deine with Fahrkarte, and deiner follows auf for a location.
Travel ticket; Fahrkarten is plural.
To ask; fragt means Mia asks.
Yes; confirms or agrees with what someone says.
Here; points to the ticket or the writing on it.
To say; sagt is used with one speaker.
He; refers to Paul.
To take; nimmt means he takes the ticket out of his backpack.
The; die is used with feminine nouns and plural nouns in this story.
Out of; followed by the dative case in aus seinem Rucksack.
His; seinem refers to Paul's backpack after aus, and seine refers to his ticket as a direct object.
To look at something; Mia looks at her ticket.
Her or their; ihre means Mia's here, while ihren means the two friends' after mit.
My; Mein goes with the masculine noun Zug, and Meine with the feminine noun Fahrkarte.
Train.
Where to; asks about a destination rather than a current location.
To read; liest is the present-tense form for one person.
To look at someone; this separable verb places an after the person being looked at.
I; the speaker refers to himself.
Also or too; Paul also wants to go to Berlin.
To show; Zeig is an informal command to one person, and zeigt describes what Paul does.
To me; the dative form of ich identifies who should be shown the ticket.
To hold; hält means Mia holds her ticket beside Paul's.
Beside it; here, beside the other ticket.
To be written; steht tells which city name appears on a ticket, not where someone is standing.
On; auf deiner Fahrkarte means on your ticket. The ticket takes the dative case here.
Name; Namen is plural and refers to the city names printed on the tickets.
Once again; Paul reads the names another time.
City; Städte is the plural form, with an umlaut.
To be; ist is the present-tense form for one thing, such as the city or ticket.
Different; the city on Paul's ticket is not the same as Mia's destination.
Not; makes the statement negative.
For; identifies the destination for which a ticket is valid.
We; refers to Mia and Paul together.
Two.
Different; verschiedene describes the two cities as not being the same.
To see or notice; sieht means Paul notices a service counter.
Service or ticket counter at the station.
There; refers to the counter Paul has noticed.
To sit or be seated; sitzt describes the woman at the counter.
Woman.
To need; brauchen goes with wir here.
Help or assistance.
To nod; nickt means Mia nods in agreement.
The two of them; refers to Mia and Paul together.
To go or walk; gehen describes both friends walking to the counter.
With; followed by the dative case in mit ihren Fahrkarten.
To the; short for zu dem, used here for movement toward the counter.
